addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/apache/airflow
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: apache/airflow:3.3.1
7	  port: 8080
8	  vm: m1.mem16
9	  flavor_id: m1.mem16
10	  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0730
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: apache-airflow
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER BEFORE THE PLAN IS APPROVED, NOT AFTER. (1) THIS IS OUTSIDE THE NO-CARD FREE TRIAL. The trial caps the app VM at m1.medium and this needs m1.mem16, so it needs a card on the account. Do not start the deploy and discover it at the quota rejection. (2) THIS IS A SINGLE-MACHINE AIRFLOW. One scheduler, one api-server, tasks executing on the same VM through LocalExecutor. It is not highly available and it does not scale horizontally: if the VM goes, Airflow goes. That is an honest single-machine Airflow and not a cluster, and anyone who needs distributed workers needs more than one machine and a different recipe."
18	  - "USE LocalExecutor, AND KNOW THAT THIS IS AIRFLOW'S OWN DEFAULT RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE. config.yml:70-78 sets [core] executor to LocalExecutor by default. The upstream compose overrides it to CeleryExecutor and therefore also needs Redis, a celery worker and a flower profile, which is seven containers for a machine that can run four. Set AIRFLOW__CORE__EXECUTOR=LocalExecutor explicitly and delete the redis service and the airflow-worker service entirely. Set AIRFLOW__CORE__PARALLELISM and AIRFLOW__CORE__MAX_ACTIVE_TASKS_PER_DAG deliberately, because with LocalExecutor every task runs on this VM and the defaults assume a cluster."
19	  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: SWITCH TO THE FAB AUTH MANAGER AND CREATE THE ADMIN FROM ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES AT DEPLOY TIME, BEFORE THE HOSTNAME EXISTS. Two things make this the most important quirk in the file. First, config.yml:110-116 shows the DEFAULT auth manager is SimpleAuthManager, and that class says of itself at simple_auth_manager.py:171-183 that it stores passwords in PLAINTEXT and PRINTS THE GENERATED PASSWORD TO STDOUT AND THE LOGS on first init, with a default user list of admin holding the admin role (config.yml:117-131). An instance left on it has an admin whose password is sitting in docker logs and in a JSON file, with no way to change it in the UI. Second, the upstream compose's init container creates the first account from _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_USERNAME and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_PASSWORD, whose documented defaults are both the word airflow. So: set AIRFLOW__CORE__AUTH_MANAGER to airflow.providers.fab.auth_manager.fab_auth_manager.FabAuthManager (the provider is already in the official image, which is why the upstream compose uses it with no extra install), set _AIRFLOW_DB_MIGRATE and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_CREATE to true on the init container, and set the username and an ALPHANUMERIC generated password yourself. The admin then exists before the URL is reachable and nobody can claim it."
20	  - "IS REGISTRATION OPEN AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT? NO. Airflow has no self-service signup at all under either auth manager: further accounts are created by an admin in the UI under Security, or by the airflow users create CLI. There is no setting to close because there is no door. The only ownership risk is the two defaults in the previous quirk, and both are closed at deploy time."
21	  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS VISITOR CAN REACH, VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. core_api/routes/public/__init__.py:55-104 registers an authenticated_router carrying Depends(get_user) as a defence-in-depth backstop, and puts dags, dag_sources, connections, variables, xcom, config, task instances, logs, pools, plugins and providers on it. Only three routers sit outside it: monitor (GET /api/v2/monitor/health), version (GET /api/v2/version) and auth (the login endpoints). So on a correctly configured instance an anonymous caller gets the health payload, the version string and a login form, and nothing else. The check script in this file asserts exactly that, in both directions."
22	  - "⛔ SET AIRFLOW__CORE__FERNET_KEY EXPLICITLY AND REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY. config.yml:231-238 describes it as the secret key that saves connection passwords in the database, and its shipped default is the placeholder {FERNET_KEY} rather than a value. Every Connection password and every encrypted Variable in the metadata database is sealed with it, so a redeploy that generates a different one leaves that data in the database and permanently undecryptable, while Airflow itself starts perfectly. Generate it with the library Airflow itself uses, from inside the image, so the format is right by construction: sudo docker run --rm apache/airflow:3.3.1 python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())'. Store it with the deployment, never in this file."
23	  - "SET THE OTHER TWO SECRETS TOO, AND SET THEM THE SAME ACROSS EVERY CONTAINER. AIRFLOW__API_AUTH__JWT_SECRET is what the scheduler and the api-server use to authenticate to each other; config.yml:2169+ says it must be consistent across all components that generate or validate tokens, and recommends passing it by environment variable rather than a config file. The upstream compose defaults it to a literal placeholder string, which is exactly the sort of default that ships to production unnoticed. AIRFLOW__API__SECRET_KEY (config.yml:1641-1652) signs the api server's session; changing it logs everyone out. Generate both, put them in the shared environment block so every service gets the identical value, and reuse them on redeploys."
24	  - "⛔ BUILD THE DATABASE URL YOURSELF, DO NOT PASTE REDU'S DATABASE_URL IN. Airflow reads AIRFLOW__DATABASE__SQL_ALCHEMY_CONN, and the upstream compose writes it as postgresql+psycopg://... The dialect suffix is load-bearing: redu injects PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD and a plain postgresql:// DATABASE_URL into the project .env, and the plain form lets SQLAlchemy pick a driver by its own default rather than the one upstream tests against. Compose it from the PG* five as postgresql+psycopg://${PGUSER}:[REDACTED:conn-password]@${PGHOST}:${PGPORT}/${PGDATABASE} in the shared environment block. Remember deploy_compose only APPENDS those variables to the project .env; it never edits your compose, so the compose has to interpolate them itself."
25	  - "ONE DATABASE, NO SUPERUSER, NO SECOND SERVER. Worth stating because it broke two entries in this library: redu's managed Postgres serves exactly ONE database and refuses any other at authentication with SQLSTATE 28000, superuser or not. Airflow with LocalExecutor uses a single metadata database and creates nothing else. (With CeleryExecutor it also wants a result backend, which the upstream compose points at the SAME database, so even that would not need a second one. It still needs Redis, which is the actual reason not to.) So database:'managed' with the default role, no db_superuser, no db_extensions."
26	  - "⛔ THE MIGRATION AND THE ADMIN COME FROM A ONE-SHOT INIT CONTAINER THAT MUST FINISH FIRST. Keep the airflow-init service: it runs as user 0:0, creates /opt/airflow/{logs,dags,plugins,config} if missing, CHOWNS the whole tree to the airflow uid, and with _AIRFLOW_DB_MIGRATE and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_CREATE set it migrates the schema and creates the admin. Every long-lived service must declare depends_on airflow-init with condition service_completed_successfully. Drop it and you get four containers racing an unmigrated database and a directory tree owned by root."
27	  - "RUN AS THE AIRFLOW UID AND KEEP THE FOUR SHARED PATHS ON THE SAME VOLUMES. Set user to 50000:0 on every Airflow service, as the upstream compose does, and mount /opt/airflow/dags, /opt/airflow/logs, /opt/airflow/config and /opt/airflow/plugins so that all four containers see the SAME storage. The scheduler writes task logs there and the api-server reads them back to render them in the UI; put them on different volumes and the logs simply do not appear, with no error anywhere."
28	  - "⛔ YOUR DAGS SHIP IN THE UPLOAD, AND THAT IS THE PRACTICAL LIMIT OF THIS RECIPE. Put a dags/ directory next to your docker-compose.yml before prepare_upload and bind-mount it at /opt/airflow/dags. The dag-processor picks up new and changed files on disk by itself, so adding a DAG afterwards means either another deploy or SSHing to the VM and writing the file. If the user expects to edit DAGs from a git repository continuously, the real answer is a git-sync sidecar or a CI job that writes to the VM, and neither is in this recipe. Say that out loud rather than letting them find out on their second DAG."
29	  - "SET AIRFLOW__CORE__LOAD_EXAMPLES=False AND AIRFLOW__API__BASE_URL. config.yml:196-211 notes that the official Docker image already sets LOAD_EXAMPLES to False, and that the upstream compose turns it back ON; a public instance does not want dozens of example DAGs it did not ask for. And config.yml:1695-1702 says plainly that Airflow cannot guess your domain, so set AIRFLOW__API__BASE_URL to https://<your-dname>. Generate the dname yourself in full <app>-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form before deploying, since this has to be right at first boot."
30	  - "LEAVE [api] expose_config AND [core] test_connection ALONE. config.yml:1655-1662 defaults expose_config to False, which hides the configuration from the web UI, and config.yml:511-525 defaults test_connection to Disabled with upstream's own note that connection testing can be done maliciously. Both defaults are the safe ones on a public hostname. Do not enable either to make debugging easier and then forget."
31	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE, AND THE ONE FIGURE UPSTREAM PUBLISHES IS A FLOOR RATHER THAN A MEASUREMENT. The upstream compose's init container prints a warning when available memory is under 4000 MB, when there are fewer than 2 CPUs, or when there is less than 10 GB of disk, and that is stated for the SEVEN-container Celery stack. This recipe runs four Airflow processes instead of six, but every one of them loads the whole Airflow Python runtime, and with LocalExecutor the TASKS run on this machine too. m1.mem16 (4 vCPU / 16 GB, 40 GB disk) is reasoning from that, not a measurement: m1.medium's 4 GB would sit exactly on upstream's warning line with nothing left for a task. Disk matters as much as memory here, because task logs accumulate under /opt/airflow/logs forever unless something prunes them. Measure idle memory, memory under one real DAG run, and disk growth on the first run, and write all three back into this file."
32	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> tell the user this is OUTSIDE the free trial and is a single-machine Airflow, and get their yes to both -> generate the dname -> put your dags/ directory beside the compose -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.073/hr, roughly GBP 53 a month) and WAIT -> deploy_compose with flavor_id 'm1.mem16', database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the database VM to the app flavor, which here would nearly double an already large bill), port 8080. Pass the flavor by NAME: the MCP resolves names to ids at its single mutating chokepoint, and m1.mem16's id has not been confirmed on a real deploy the way '2', '3' and '4' have."
33	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write your own docker-compose.yml plus a dags/ directory locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. ⛔ Do NOT clone this repository: it is one of the largest monorepos on GitHub and none of it is needed to run a pulled image."
34	  - "⛔ DO NOT COPY THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE. airflow-core/docs/howto/docker-compose/docker-compose.yaml is a documentation example and its own header says: WARNING, this configuration is for local development, do not use it in a production deployment. Concretely it ships a bundled postgres:16 with a hardcoded credential, a Redis, a Celery worker, a flower profile, LOAD_EXAMPLES turned on, and a placeholder JWT secret. Use it as a reference for the environment block and the service commands (api-server, scheduler, dag-processor, triggerer), and write your own file."
35	  - "PORT 8080, from the api-server. Health probe: GET /api/v2/monitor/health, which is one of only three anonymous endpoints and returns a JSON body naming the health of the metadata database, the scheduler, the triggerer and the dag-processor. That makes it a genuinely useful check rather than a liveness ping: a 200 with a scheduler reported unhealthy is a real answer. First boot is slow, since the image is large and the schema migration runs before anything serves."
36	  - "LICENCE: Apache License 2.0, unmodified, verified from the LICENSE file. Permissive, with a patent grant and an attribution requirement; nothing to reason about for a self-hoster. Note the trademark: the Apache Software Foundation owns the Airflow name, so do not rebrand a hosted instance as an Airflow product."
37	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. The Fernet key, the JWT secret, the api secret key and the admin password all belong in the session handover and in the deployment's environment, never in a committed recipe. Record that an admin was created at deploy time, never the values."

  - "⛔⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER BEFORE THE PLAN IS APPROVED, NOT AFTER. (1) THIS IS OUTSIDE THE NO-CARD FREE TRIAL.   - "USE LocalExecutor, AND KNOW THAT THIS IS AIRFLOW'S OWN DEFAULT RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE. config.yml:70-78 sets [core] executor to LocalExecutor by default.   - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: SWITCH TO THE FAB AUTH MANAGER AND CREATE THE ADMIN FROM ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES AT DEPLOY TIME, BEFORE THE HOSTNAME EXISTS. First, config.yml:110-116 shows the DEFAULT auth manager is SimpleAuthManager, and that class says of itself at simple_auth_manager.py:171-183 that it stores passwords in PLAINTEXT and PRINTS THE GENERATED PASSWORD TO STDOUT AND THE LOGS on first init, with a default user list of admin holding the admin role (config.yml:117-131). Second, the upstream compose's init container creates the first account from _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_USERNAME and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_PASSWORD, whose documented defaults are both the word airflow.   - "ONE DATABASE, NO SUPERUSER, NO SECOND SERVER. Airflow with LocalExecutor uses a single metadata database and creates nothing else. (With CeleryExecutor it also wants a result backend, which the upstream compose points at the SAME database, so even that would not need a second one.   - "⛔ THE MIGRATION AND THE ADMIN COME FROM A ONE-SHOT INIT CONTAINER THAT MUST FINISH FIRST. Drop it and you get four containers racing an unmigrated database and a directory tree owned by root."
  - "RUN AS THE AIRFLOW UID AND KEEP THE FOUR SHARED PATHS ON THE SAME VOLUMES.   - "⛔ YOUR DAGS SHIP IN THE UPLOAD, AND THAT IS THE PRACTICAL LIMIT OF THIS RECIPE. # Self-host Apache Airflow on redu

Author, schedule and monitor workflows on a machine you own: four Airflow processes on one VM with
LocalExecutor, a managed Postgres holding the metadata, and a public HTTPS URL.

## Read this before you deploy

**This is outside the no-card free trial.** It needs an m1.mem16 VM and the trial caps the app VM
at m1.medium, so it needs a card on the account. About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month.

Airflow's own default executor, so nothing here is downgraded: the scheduler runs your tasks as
local processes. What you do not get is high availability or horizontal scale. One scheduler, one
api-server, one VM. If you need distributed workers, you need more than one machine and this is

## What this deploys

- **api-server** on port 8080, the UI and the REST API, public on its own hostname with TLS.
- **scheduler**, **dag-processor** and **triggerer** beside it on the same VM.
- A one-shot **init** container that migrates the schema and creates the admin account from
  environment variables before anything is reachable.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding every DAG run, Connection and Variable.
- Volumes for `dags`, `logs`, `config` and `plugins`, shared by all four containers.

No Redis and no Celery worker: dropping them is returning to Airflow's default, not cutting a
corner.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Put your
`dags/` directory beside this file, then:

    Read redu.md and deploy Apache Airflow on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The auth manager.** Airflow's default one says of itself, in its own source, that it stores
passwords in plaintext and prints the generated password into the logs. The recipe switches to the
FAB auth manager and creates the admin from environment variables at deploy time, so the account
exists before the URL does and its password is never in a log.

**The Fernet key.** Every Connection password and encrypted Variable in the metadata database is
sealed with it. Redeploy with a different one and that data stays in the database, permanently
undecryptable, while Airflow starts up looking perfectly healthy.

**The shared paths.** The scheduler writes task logs and the api-server reads them back to render
them. Put those two on different volumes and the logs just never appear in the UI, with no error
anywhere.

## Check what an anonymous visitor can reach

Mind the polarity of the second call. A protected endpoint answering **401 or 403 is the pass**. A
200 there means authentication is off. A 404 means the route moved and the check told you nothing,
which is not the same as a pass.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Is this Airflow actually asking for credentials?
# usage: ./check.sh <host>.redu.cloud   (no scheme)
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: check.sh <host>.redu.cloud}"
BODY=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$BODY"' EXIT

# (1) POSITIVE: /api/v2/version is anonymous BY DESIGN, so it answers on a correctly locked
#     instance too. That is what makes it a liveness probe rather than a security check.
#     redu's edge answers 502 for the first minutes while the image is pulled and migrated.
code=$(curl -sS -L -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v2/version")
if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $code from the edge. Still starting; Airflow's first boot is slow."
  exit 3
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"version"' "$BODY"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v2/version answered $code without a version payload."
  echo "              This is not Airflow talking. Read nothing into step 2."
  exit 3
fi

# (2) The real test. /api/v2/variables sits on the authenticated router, so an anonymous
#     request to it must be refused. Variables are where people keep their secrets.
probe=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  "https://$HOST/api/v2/variables")
case "$probe" in
  401|403)
    echo "OK: anonymous access to the Variables API is refused ($probe)."
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous caller just read your Variables ($probe)."
    echo "      The auth manager is not enforcing anything. Take this instance down now."
    exit 1
    ;;
  404)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 404. The endpoint moved, so this check proved nothing at all."
    echo "              Verify by hand and do not leave the instance up until you have."
    exit 3
    ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $probe. Do not leave this instance running until you know why."
    exit 3
    ;;
```

# Apache Airflow 3.3.1 on a single redu VM, LocalExecutor, managed Postgres.
# Written for redu (see redu.md) — deliberately NOT the upstream local-development compose.
# No bundled postgres, no redis, no celery worker, no flower.
#
# PGHOST/PGPORT/PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD and the AIRFLOW_* secrets below are
# appended to the project .env by redu at deploy time; this file interpolates them.

x-airflow-common: &airflow-common
  image: apache/airflow:3.3.1
  environment: &airflow-common-env
    # --- executor: Airflow's own default. Every task runs on this VM. ---
    AIRFLOW__CORE__EXECUTOR: LocalExecutor
    AIRFLOW__CORE__PARALLELISM: "8"
    AIRFLOW__CORE__MAX_ACTIVE_TASKS_PER_DAG: "4"

    # --- metadata database: composed from the PG* five, psycopg dialect is load-bearing ---
    AIRFLOW__DATABASE__SQL_ALCHEMY_CONN: postgresql+psycopg://${PGUSER}:[REDACTED:conn-password]@${PGHOST}:${PGPORT}/${PGDATABASE}

    # --- auth: FAB, not the default SimpleAuthManager (which logs a plaintext password) ---
    AIRFLOW__CORE__AUTH_MANAGER: airflow.providers.fab.auth_manager.fab_auth_manager.FabAuthManager

    # --- the three secrets, identical in every container ---
    AIRFLOW__CORE__FERNET_KEY: ${AIRFLOW_FERNET_KEY}
    AIRFLOW__API_AUTH__JWT_SECRET: [REDACTED:value]}
    AIRFLOW__API__SECRET_KEY: [REDACTED:value]}

    # --- this instance's own public identity; Airflow cannot guess it ---
    AIRFLOW__API__BASE_URL: ${AIRFLOW_BASE_URL}

    # --- the DAG list is the user's own ---
    AIRFLOW__CORE__LOAD_EXAMPLES: "False"

    # [api] expose_config and [core] test_connection are left at their safe defaults.
  volumes:
    - ./dags:/opt/airflow/dags
    - airflow-logs:/opt/airflow/logs
    - airflow-config:/opt/airflow/config
    - airflow-plugins:/opt/airflow/plugins
  user: "50000:0"
  depends_on:
    airflow-init:
      condition: service_completed_successfully

services:
  # One-shot: creates the four shared paths, chowns the tree, migrates the schema and
  # creates the admin — all before anything is reachable.
  airflow-init:
    image: apache/airflow:3.3.1
    entrypoint: /bin/bash
    command:
      - -c
      - |
        mkdir -p /opt/airflow/logs /opt/airflow/dags /opt/airflow/plugins /opt/airflow/config
        chown -R "50000:0" /opt/airflow/logs /opt/airflow/dags /opt/airflow/plugins /opt/airflow/config
        exec /entrypoint airflow version
    environment:
      <<: *airflow-common-env
      _AIRFLOW_DB_MIGRATE: "true"
      _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_CREATE: "true"
      _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_USERNAME: ${AIRFLOW_ADMIN_USERNAME}
      _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_PASSWORD: [REDACTED:value]}
    volumes:
      - ./dags:/opt/airflow/dags
      - airflow-logs:/opt/airflow/logs
      - airflow-config:/opt/airflow/config
      - airflow-plugins:/opt/airflow/plugins
    user: "0:0"
    restart: "no"

  airflow-apiserver:
    <<: *airflow-common
    command: api-server
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    restart: always

  airflow-scheduler:
    <<: *airflow-common
    command: scheduler
    restart: always

  airflow-dag-processor:
    <<: *airflow-common
    command: dag-processor
    restart: always

  airflow-triggerer:
    <<: *airflow-common
    command: triggerer
    restart: always

volumes:
  airflow-logs:
  airflow-config:
  airflow-plugins:

That is an honest single-machine Airflow and not a cluster, and anyone who needs distributed workers needs more than one machine and a different recipe."

Set AIRFLOW__CORE__EXECUTOR=LocalExecutor explicitly and delete the redis service and the airflow-worker service entirely. First, config.yml:110-116 shows the DEFAULT auth manager is SimpleAuthManager, and that class says of itself at simple_auth_manager.py:171-183 that it stores passwords in PLAINTEXT and PRINTS THE GENERATED PASSWORD TO STDOUT AND THE LOGS on first init, with a default user list of admin holding the admin role (config.yml:117-131). An instance left on it has an admin whose password is sitting in docker logs and in a JSON file, with no way to change it in the UI. Second, the upstream compose's init container creates the first account from _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_USERNAME and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_PASSWORD, whose documented defaults are both the word airflow. So: set AIRFLOW__CORE__AUTH_MANAGER to airflow.providers.fab.auth_manager.fab_auth_manager.FabAuthManager (the provider is already in the official image, which is why the upstream compose uses it with no extra install), set _AIRFLOW_DB_MIGRATE and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_CREATE to true on the init container, and set the username and an ALPHANUMERIC generated password yourself.   - "IS REGISTRATION OPEN AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT? NO. Airflow has no self-service signup at all under either auth manager: further accounts are created by an admin in the UI under Security, or by the airflow users create CLI. There is no setting to close because there is no door. The only ownership risk is the two defaults in the previous quirk, and both are closed at deploy time."

Only three routers sit outside it: monitor (GET /api/v2/monitor/health), version (GET /api/v2/version) and auth (the login endpoints). So on a correctly configured instance an anonymous caller gets the health payload, the version string and a login form, and nothing else. The check script in this file asserts exactly that, in both directions."

Every Connection password and every encrypted Variable in the metadata database is sealed with it, so a redeploy that generates a different one leaves that data in the database and permanently undecryptable, while Airflow itself starts perfectly. Generate it with the library Airflow itself uses, from inside the image, so the format is right by construction: sudo docker run --rm apache/airflow:3.3.1 python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())'. # Self-host Apache Airflow on redu

Author, schedule and monitor workflows on a machine you own: four Airflow processes on one VM with
LocalExecutor, a managed Postgres holding the metadata, and a public HTTPS URL.

## Read this before you deploy

**This is outside the no-card free trial.** It needs an m1.mem16 VM and the trial caps the app VM
at m1.medium, so it needs a card on the account. About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month.

**This is a single-machine Airflow, and that is what LocalExecutor is for.** LocalExecutor is
Airflow's own default executor, so nothing here is downgraded: the scheduler runs your tasks as
local processes. What you do not get is high availability or horizontal scale. One scheduler, one
api-server, one VM. If you need distributed workers, you need more than one machine and this is
not the recipe for it.

## What this deploys

- **api-server** on port 8080, the UI and the REST API, public on its own hostname with TLS.
- **scheduler**, **dag-processor** and **triggerer** beside it on the same VM.
- A one-shot **init** container that migrates the schema and creates the admin account from
  environment variables before anything is reachable.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding every DAG run, Connection and Variable.
- Volumes for `dags`, `logs`, `config` and `plugins`, shared by all four containers.

No Redis and no Celery worker: dropping them is returning to Airflow's default, not cutting a
corner.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Put your
`dags/` directory beside this file, then:

    Read redu.md and deploy Apache Airflow on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The auth manager.** Airflow's default one says of itself, in its own source, that it stores
passwords in plaintext and prints the generated password into the logs. The recipe switches to the
FAB auth manager and creates the admin from environment variables at deploy time, so the account
exists before the URL does and its password is never in a log.

**The Fernet key.** Every Connection password and encrypted Variable in the metadata database is
sealed with it. Redeploy with a different one and that data stays in the database, permanently
undecryptable, while Airflow starts up looking perfectly healthy.

**The shared paths.** The scheduler writes task logs and the api-server reads them back to render
them. Put those two on different volumes and the logs just never appear in the UI, with no error
anywhere.

## Check what an anonymous visitor can reach

Mind the polarity of the second call. A protected endpoint answering **401 or 403 is the pass**. A
200 there means authentication is off. A 404 means the route moved and the check told you nothing,
which is not the same as a pass.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Is this Airflow actually asking for credentials?
# usage: ./check.sh <host>.redu.cloud   (no scheme)
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: check.sh <host>.redu.cloud}"
BODY=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$BODY"' EXIT

# (1) POSITIVE: /api/v2/version is anonymous BY DESIGN, so it answers on a correctly locked
#     instance too. That is what makes it a liveness probe rather than a security check.
#     redu's edge answers 502 for the first minutes while the image is pulled and migrated.
code=$(curl -sS -L -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v2/version")
if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $code from the edge. Still starting; Airflow's first boot is slow."
  exit 3
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"version"' "$BODY"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v2/version answered $code without a version payload."
  echo "              This is not Airflow talking. Read nothing into step 2."
  exit 3
fi

# (2) The real test. /api/v2/variables sits on the authenticated router, so an anonymous
#     request to it must be refused. Variables are where people keep their secrets.
probe=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  "https://$HOST/api/v2/variables")
case "$probe" in
  401|403)
    echo "OK: anonymous access to the Variables API is refused ($probe)."
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous caller just read your Variables ($probe)."
    echo "      The auth manager is not enforcing anything. Take this instance down now."
    exit 1
    ;;
  404)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 404. The endpoint moved, so this check proved nothing at all."
    echo "              Verify by hand and do not leave the instance up until you have."
    exit 3
    ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $probe. Do not leave this instance running until you know why."
    exit 3
    ;;
esac

# (3) The health payload names each component, so read it rather than just counting a 200.
curl -sS -L "https://$HOST/api/v2/monitor/health"
echo
```

## Prove the auth manager and the database are the ones you asked for

On the app VM over SSH. Both halves: the positive line is what makes the zero on the negative one
mean anything.

```bash
set -u
C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -iE 'apiserver|api-server' | head -1)
if [ -z "$C" ]; then
  echo "no Airflow api-server container is running; nothing below would mean anything"
  exit 1
fi

# POSITIVE: the FAB auth manager must actually be the configured one. A match here also proves
# this exec reached a real container, which a lone zero-count grep never establishes.
echo -n "FabAuthManager configured (expect >= 1): "
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv AIRFLOW__CORE__AUTH_MANAGER | grep -c 'FabAuthManager'

# NEGATIVE, and only meaningful because the line above was not zero: the dev-only auth manager
# writes its plaintext password file into AIRFLOW_HOME on first init.
echo -n "SimpleAuthManager plaintext password file (expect 0): "
sudo docker exec "$C" sh -c 'ls /opt/airflow/simple_auth_manager_passwords.json.generated 2>/dev/null | wc -l'

# POSITIVE: the metadata connection points at the private managed database VM, with the psycopg
# dialect, and not at a container on this host.
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv AIRFLOW__DATABASE__SQL_ALCHEMY_CONN | sed 's#//[^@]*@#//<redacted>@#'

# POSITIVE: no bundled postgres and no redis snuck in from the upstream compose.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'

# POSITIVE: the example DAGs are off, so the DAG list is the user's own.
echo -n "load_examples (expect False): "
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv AIRFLOW__CORE__LOAD_EXAMPLES
```

preflight.do: This app is told its OWN url (BASE_URL / SITE_URL / callback / hostname env detected). Generate the dname UP FRONT and pass it as `dname`, wiring that exact value into the env - do not let redu auto-generate the URL.
preflight.why: 44 of 46 real deploys carrying env embedded their own redu.cloud URL. redu appends a random 8-char suffix to a bare name, so an auto-generated URL will NOT match anything you wired, and a redeploy changes it again - silently breaking OAuth callbacks and cookies.

preflight.do: Does this app CREATE its schema on first boot? If not, pass migrate_command - otherwise it deploys, passes the probe, and 502s on real use.
preflight.why: #1: deploy-but-502 is the classic database-backed failure. Auto-migrating apps need nothing; the rest need one command. Asking is stack-independent; guessing the framework is not.

preflight.do: Expect a slow start; redu time-boxes `up -d` and lets the external probe decide. Do NOT retry on a 'building' status before the probe window closes.
preflight.why: #9/#16: `up -d` blocks on the health/one-shot chain and pinned SigNoz in 'building' for 27 min; podman also aborted Tracecat's gated services.

preflight.do: ~10 services detected - size the VM up and expect a 10-20 min settle.
preflight.why: #22: heavy stacks legitimately take 10-20 min; SigNoz was also RAM-starved at a small flavor.

Everything is prepared; nothing has been created yet. Two things `redu.md` insists I tell you **before** you approve:

**1. This is outside the no-card free trial.** The trial caps the app VM at m1.medium; this recipe needs **m1.mem16**, so the account needs a card on it. If there's no card, the deploy will be rejected at the quota gate rather than half-built.

**2. This is a single-machine Airflow.** One scheduler, one api-server, one dag-processor, one triggerer, and your tasks executing on that same VM via LocalExecutor. LocalExecutor is Airflow's own default, so nothing is downgraded — but there is no high availability and no horizontal scale. If the VM goes, Airflow goes. Distributed workers need more than one machine and a different recipe.

**The plan** (written to `redu-deploy-plan.md`):

| Resource | Size | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| App VM (5 containers: init + api-server, scheduler, dag-processor, triggerer) | m1.mem16 — 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 40 GB | GBP 0.0556/hr |
| Managed Postgres, own private VM, private-only | m1.small — 1 vCPU / 2 GB | GBP 0.0174/hr |
| **Total** | | **GBP 0.073/hr ≈ GBP 53.29/mo** |

Quota fits (2 instances, 5 vCPU, 18 GB against 10/20/50). Public URL pinned up front: **https://airflow-xsw6juud.redu.cloud**

What I've written locally: my own `docker-compose.yml` (not the upstream local-dev one — no bundled postgres, no Redis, no Celery worker), plus a `dags/` directory containing one trivial `hello_redu` DAG so the instance has something to show. Fernet key, JWT secret, api secret key and an alphanumeric admin password are already generated and held outside the repo; the admin (`airflow-admin`) is created by the init container before the URL is reachable.

One limit worth knowing now: **your DAGs ship in the upload.** Adding a DAG later means another deploy or SSHing to the VM. Continuous DAG editing from a git repo needs a git-sync sidecar or a CI job, and neither is in this recipe.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Is this Airflow actually asking for credentials?
# usage: ./check.sh <host>.redu.cloud   (no scheme)
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: check.sh <host>.redu.cloud}"
BODY=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$BODY"' EXIT

# (1) POSITIVE: /api/v2/version is anonymous BY DESIGN, so it answers on a correctly locked
#     instance too. That is what makes it a liveness probe rather than a security check.
#     redu's edge answers 502 for the first minutes while the image is pulled and migrated.
code=$(curl -sS -L -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v2/version")
if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $code from the edge. Still starting; Airflow's first boot is slow."
  exit 3
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"version"' "$BODY"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v2/version answered $code without a version payload."
  echo "              This is not Airflow talking. Read nothing into step 2."
  exit 3
fi

# (2) The real test. /api/v2/variables sits on the authenticated router, so an anonymous
#     request to it must be refused. Variables are where people keep their secrets.
probe=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  "https://$HOST/api/v2/variables")
case "$probe" in
  401|403)
    echo "OK: anonymous access to the Variables API is refused ($probe)."
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous caller just read your Variables ($probe)."
    echo "      The auth manager is not enforcing anything. Take this instance down now."
    exit 1
    ;;
  404)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 404. The endpoint moved, so this check proved nothing at all."
    echo "              Verify by hand and do not leave the instance up until you have."
    exit 3
    ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $probe. Do not leave this instance running until you know why."
    exit 3
    ;;
esac

# (3) The health payload names each component, so read it rather than just counting a 200.
curl -sS -L "https://$HOST/api/v2/monitor/health"
echo

input.redu_md:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/apache/airflow
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: apache/airflow:3.3.1
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.mem16
  flavor_id: m1.mem16
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0730
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: apache-airflow
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER BEFORE THE PLAN IS APPROVED, NOT AFTER. (1) THIS IS OUTSIDE THE NO-CARD FREE TRIAL. The trial caps the app VM at m1.medium and this needs m1.mem16, so it needs a card on the account. Do not start the deploy and discover it at the quota rejection. (2) THIS IS A SINGLE-MACHINE AIRFLOW. One scheduler, one api-server, tasks executing on the same VM through LocalExecutor. It is not highly available and it does not scale horizontally: if the VM goes, Airflow goes. That is an honest single-machine Airflow and not a cluster, and anyone who needs distributed workers needs more than one machine and a different recipe."
  - "USE LocalExecutor, AND KNOW THAT THIS IS AIRFLOW'S OWN DEFAULT RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE. config.yml:70-78 sets [core] executor to LocalExecutor by default. The upstream compose overrides it to CeleryExecutor and therefore also needs Redis, a celery worker and a flower profile, which is seven containers for a machine that can run four. Set AIRFLOW__CORE__EXECUTOR=LocalExecutor explicitly and delete the redis service and the airflow-worker service entirely. Set AIRFLOW__CORE__PARALLELISM and AIRFLOW__CORE__MAX_ACTIVE_TASKS_PER_DAG deliberately, because with LocalExecutor every task runs on this VM and the defaults assume a cluster."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: SWITCH TO THE FAB AUTH MANAGER AND CREATE THE ADMIN FROM ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES AT DEPLOY TIME, BEFORE THE HOSTNAME EXISTS. Two things make this the most important quirk in the file. First, config.yml:110-116 shows the DEFAULT auth manager is SimpleAuthManager, and that class says of itself at simple_auth_manager.py:171-183 that it stores passwords in PLAINTEXT and PRINTS THE GENERATED PASSWORD TO STDOUT AND THE LOGS on first init, with a default user list of admin holding the admin role (config.yml:117-131). An instance left on it has an admin whose password is sitting in docker logs and in a JSON file, with no way to change it in the UI. Second, the upstream compose's init container creates the first account from _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_USERNAME and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_PASSWORD, whose documented defaults are both the word airflow. So: set AIRFLOW__CORE__AUTH_MANAGER to airflow.providers.fab.auth_manager.fab_auth_manager.FabAuthManager (the provider is already in the official image, which is why the upstream compose uses it with no extra install), set _AIRFLOW_DB_MIGRATE and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_CREATE to true on the init container, and set the username and an ALPHANUMERIC generated password yourself. The admin then exists before the URL is reachable and nobody can claim it."
  - "IS REGISTRATION OPEN AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT? NO. Airflow has no self-service signup at all under either auth manager: further accounts are created by an admin in the UI under Security, or by the airflow users create CLI. There is no setting to close because there is no door. The only ownership risk is the two defaults in the previous quirk, and both are closed at deploy time."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS VISITOR CAN REACH, VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. core_api/routes/public/__init__.py:55-104 registers an authenticated_router carrying Depends(get_user) as a defence-in-depth backstop, and puts dags, dag_sources, connections, variables, xcom, config, task instances, logs, pools, plugins and providers on it. Only three routers sit outside it: monitor (GET /api/v2/monitor/health), version (GET /api/v2/version) and auth (the login endpoints). So on a correctly configured instance an anonymous caller gets the health payload, the version string and a login form, and nothing else. The check script in this file asserts exactly that, in both directions."
  - "⛔ SET AIRFLOW__CORE__FERNET_KEY EXPLICITLY AND REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY. config.yml:231-238 describes it as the secret key that saves connection passwords in the database, and its shipped default is the placeholder {FERNET_KEY} rather than a value. Every Connection password and every encrypted Variable in the metadata database is sealed with it, so a redeploy that generates a different one leaves that data in the database and permanently undecryptable, while Airflow itself starts perfectly. Generate it with the library Airflow itself uses, from inside the image, so the format is right by construction: sudo docker run --rm apache/airflow:3.3.1 python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())'. Store it with the deployment, never in this file."
  - "SET THE OTHER TWO SECRETS TOO, AND SET THEM THE SAME ACROSS EVERY CONTAINER. AIRFLOW__API_AUTH__JWT_SECRET is what the scheduler and the api-server use to authenticate to each other; config.yml:2169+ says it must be consistent across all components that generate or validate tokens, and recommends passing it by environment variable rather than a config file. The upstream compose defaults it to a literal placeholder string, which is exactly the sort of default that ships to production unnoticed. AIRFLOW__API__SECRET_KEY (config.yml:1641-1652) signs the api server's session; changing it logs everyone out. Generate both, put them in the shared environment block so every service gets the identical value, and reuse them on redeploys."
  - "⛔ BUILD THE DATABASE URL YOURSELF, DO NOT PASTE REDU'S DATABASE_URL IN. Airflow reads AIRFLOW__DATABASE__SQL_ALCHEMY_CONN, and the upstream compose writes it as postgresql+psycopg://... The dialect suffix is load-bearing: redu injects PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD and a plain postgresql:// DATABASE_URL into the project .env, and the plain form lets SQLAlchemy pick a driver by its own default rather than the one upstream tests against. Compose it from the PG* five as postgresql+psycopg://${PGUSER}:[REDACTED:conn-password]@${PGHOST}:${PGPORT}/${PGDATABASE} in the shared environment block. Remember deploy_compose only APPENDS those variables to the project .env; it never edits your compose, so the compose has to interpolate them itself."
  - "ONE DATABASE, NO SUPERUSER, NO SECOND SERVER. Worth stating because it broke two entries in this library: redu's managed Postgres serves exactly ONE database and refuses any other at authentication with SQLSTATE 28000, superuser or not. Airflow with LocalExecutor uses a single metadata database and creates nothing else. (With CeleryExecutor it also wants a result backend, which the upstream compose points at the SAME database, so even that would not need a second one. It still needs Redis, which is the actual reason not to.) So database:'managed' with the default role, no db_superuser, no db_extensions."
  - "⛔ THE MIGRATION AND THE ADMIN COME FROM A ONE-SHOT INIT CONTAINER THAT MUST FINISH FIRST. Keep the airflow-init service: it runs as user 0:0, creates /opt/airflow/{logs,dags,plugins,config} if missing, CHOWNS the whole tree to the airflow uid, and with _AIRFLOW_DB_MIGRATE and _AIRFLOW_WWW_USER_CREATE set it migrates the schema and creates the admin. Every long-lived service must declare depends_on airflow-init with condition service_completed_successfully. Drop it and you get four containers racing an unmigrated database and a directory tree owned by root."
  - "RUN AS THE AIRFLOW UID AND KEEP THE FOUR SHARED PATHS ON THE SAME VOLUMES. Set user to 50000:0 on every Airflow service, as the upstream compose does, and mount /opt/airflow/dags, /opt/airflow/logs, /opt/airflow/config and /opt/airflow/plugins so that all four containers see the SAME storage. The scheduler writes task logs there and the api-server reads them back to render them in the UI; put them on different volumes and the logs simply do not appear, with no error anywhere."
  - "⛔ YOUR DAGS SHIP IN THE UPLOAD, AND THAT IS THE PRACTICAL LIMIT OF THIS RECIPE. Put a dags/ directory next to your docker-compose.yml before prepare_upload and bind-mount it at /opt/airflow/dags. The dag-processor picks up new and changed files on disk by itself, so adding a DAG afterwards means either another deploy or SSHing to the VM and writing the file. If the user expects to edit DAGs from a git repository continuously, the real answer is a git-sync sidecar or a CI job that writes to the VM, and neither is in this recipe. Say that out loud rather than letting them find out on their second DAG."
  - "SET AIRFLOW__CORE__LOAD_EXAMPLES=False AND AIRFLOW__API__BASE_URL. config.yml:196-211 notes that the official Docker image already sets LOAD_EXAMPLES to False, and that the upstream compose turns it back ON; a public instance does not want dozens of example DAGs it did not ask for. And config.yml:1695-1702 says plainly that Airflow cannot guess your domain, so set AIRFLOW__API__BASE_URL to https://<your-dname>. Generate the dname yourself in full <app>-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form before deploying, since this has to be right at first boot."
  - "LEAVE [api] expose_config AND [core] test_connection ALONE. config.yml:1655-1662 defaults expose_config to False, which hides the configuration from the web UI, and config.yml:511-525 defaults test_connection to Disabled with upstream's own note that connection testing can be done maliciously. Both defaults are the safe ones on a public hostname. Do not enable either to make debugging easier and then forget."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE, AND THE ONE FIGURE UPSTREAM PUBLISHES IS A FLOOR RATHER THAN A MEASUREMENT. The upstream compose's init container prints a warning when available memory is under 4000 MB, when there are fewer than 2 CPUs, or when there is less than 10 GB of disk, and that is stated for the SEVEN-container Celery stack. This recipe runs four Airflow processes instead of six, but every one of them loads the whole Airflow Python runtime, and with LocalExecutor the TASKS run on this machine too. m1.mem16 (4 vCPU / 16 GB, 40 GB disk) is reasoning from that, not a measurement: m1.medium's 4 GB would sit exactly on upstream's warning line with nothing left for a task. Disk matters as much as memory here, because task logs accumulate under /opt/airflow/logs forever unless something prunes them. Measure idle memory, memory under one real DAG run, and disk growth on the first run, and write all three back into this file."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> tell the user this is OUTSIDE the free trial and is a single-machine Airflow, and get their yes to both -> generate the dname -> put your dags/ directory beside the compose -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.073/hr, roughly GBP 53 a month) and WAIT -> deploy_compose with flavor_id 'm1.mem16', database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the database VM to the app flavor, which here would nearly double an already large bill), port 8080. Pass the flavor by NAME: the MCP resolves names to ids at its single mutating chokepoint, and m1.mem16's id has not been confirmed on a real deploy the way '2', '3' and '4' have."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write your own docker-compose.yml plus a dags/ directory locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. ⛔ Do NOT clone this repository: it is one of the largest monorepos on GitHub and none of it is needed to run a pulled image."
  - "⛔ DO NOT COPY THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE. airflow-core/docs/howto/docker-compose/docker-compose.yaml is a documentation example and its own header says: WARNING, this configuration is for local development, do not use it in a production deployment. Concretely it ships a bundled postgres:16 with a hardcoded credential, a Redis, a Celery worker, a flower profile, LOAD_EXAMPLES turned on, and a placeholder JWT secret. Use it as a reference for the environment block and the service commands (api-server, scheduler, dag-processor, triggerer), and write your own file."
  - "PORT 8080, from the api-server. Health probe: GET /api/v2/monitor/health, which is one of only three anonymous endpoints and returns a JSON body naming the health of the metadata database, the scheduler, the triggerer and the dag-processor. That makes it a genuinely useful check rather than a liveness ping: a 200 with a scheduler reported unhealthy is a real answer. First boot is slow, since the image is large and the schema migration runs before anything serves."
  - "LICENCE: Apache License 2.0, unmodified, verified from the LICENSE file. Permissive, with a patent grant and an attribution requirement; nothing to reason about for a self-hoster. Note the trademark: the Apache Software Foundation owns the Airflow name, so do not rebrand a hosted instance as an Airflow product."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. The Fernet key, the JWT secret, the api secret key and the admin password all belong in the session handover and in the deployment's environment, never in a committed recipe. Record that an admin was created at deploy time, never the values."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back. ⚠️ Measured on deployment 428: the merge returns redu_md_merge_mode \"in_place\" when the file is richer than redu's template, which refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and NOTHING ELSE. It does not write new quirks. The memory and disk numbers this run produces are the most valuable thing it can add, and they have to be hand-added or they are lost."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres, which holds every DAG run, task history, Connection and Variable, and that database keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. ⚠️ The DAG FILES and the task LOGS live on the app VM's volumes and go with the deployment, so the history survives while the logs behind it do not. Say that plainly before deleting, and use delete_database when the user really wants it gone."
---

# Self-host Apache Airflow on redu

Author, schedule and monitor workflows on a machine you own: four Airflow processes on one VM with
LocalExecutor, a managed Postgres holding the metadata, and a public HTTPS URL.

## Read this before you deploy

**This is outside the no-card free trial.** It needs an m1.mem16 VM and the trial caps the app VM
at m1.medium, so it needs a card on the account. About GBP 0.073/hour, roughly GBP 53 a month.

**This is a single-machine Airflow, and that is what LocalExecutor is for.** LocalExecutor is
Airflow's own default executor, so nothing here is downgraded: the scheduler runs your tasks as
local processes. What you do not get is high availability or horizontal scale. One scheduler, one
api-server, one VM. If you need distributed workers, you need more than one machine and this is
not the recipe for it.

## What this deploys

- **api-server** on port 8080, the UI and the REST API, public on its own hostname with TLS.
- **scheduler**, **dag-processor** and **triggerer** beside it on the same VM.
- A one-shot **init** container that migrates the schema and creates the admin account from
  environment variables before anything is reachable.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding every DAG run, Connection and Variable.
- Volumes for `dags`, `logs`, `config` and `plugins`, shared by all four containers.

No Redis and no Celery worker: dropping them is returning to Airflow's default, not cutting a
corner.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Put your
`dags/` directory beside this file, then:

    Read redu.md and deploy Apache Airflow on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The auth manager.** Airflow's default one says of itself, in its own source, that it stores
passwords in plaintext and prints the generated password into the logs. The recipe switches to the
FAB auth manager and creates the admin from environment variables at deploy time, so the account
exists before the URL does and its password is never in a log.

**The Fernet key.** Every Connection password and encrypted Variable in the metadata database is
sealed with it. Redeploy with a different one and that data stays in the database, permanently
undecryptable, while Airflow starts up looking perfectly healthy.

**The shared paths.** The scheduler writes task logs and the api-server reads them back to render
them. Put those two on different volumes and the logs just never appear in the UI, with no error
anywhere.

## Check what an anonymous visitor can reach

Mind the polarity of the second call. A protected endpoint answering **401 or 403 is the pass**. A
200 there means authentication is off. A 404 means the route moved and the check told you nothing,
which is not the same as a pass.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Is this Airflow actually asking for credentials?
# usage: ./check.sh <host>.redu.cloud   (no scheme)
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: check.sh <host>.redu.cloud}"
BODY=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$BODY"' EXIT

# (1) POSITIVE: /api/v2/version is anonymous BY DESIGN, so it answers on a correctly locked
#     instance too. That is what makes it a liveness probe rather than a security check.
#     redu's edge answers 502 for the first minutes while the image is pulled and migrated.
code=$(curl -sS -L -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v2/version")
if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $code from the edge. Still starting; Airflow's first boot is slow."
  exit 3
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -q '"version"' "$BODY"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/v2/version answered $code without a version payload."
  echo "              This is not Airflow talking. Read nothing into step 2."
  exit 3
fi

# (2) The real test. /api/v2/variables sits on the authenticated router, so an anonymous
#     request to it must be refused. Variables are where people keep their secrets.
probe=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  "https://$HOST/api/v2/variables")
case "$probe" in
  401|403)
    echo "OK: anonymous access to the Variables API is refused ($probe)."
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: an anonymous caller just read your Variables ($probe)."
    echo "      The auth manager is not enforcing anything. Take this instance down now."
    exit 1
    ;;
  404)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 404. The endpoint moved, so this check proved nothing at all."
    echo "              Verify by hand and do not leave the instance up until you have."
    exit 3
    ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected $probe. Do not leave this instance running until you know why."
    exit 3
    ;;
esac

# (3) The health payload names each component, so read it rather than just counting a 200.
curl -sS -L "https://$HOST/api/v2/monitor/health"
echo
```

## Prove the auth manager and the database are the ones you asked for

On the app VM over SSH. Both halves: the positive line is what makes the zero on the negative one
mean anything.

```bash
set -u
C=$(sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -iE 'apiserver|api-server' | head -1)
if [ -z "$C" ]; then
  echo "no Airflow api-server container is running; nothing below would mean anything"
  exit 1
fi

# POSITIVE: the FAB auth manager must actually be the configured one. A match here also proves
# this exec reached a real container, which a lone zero-count grep never establishes.
echo -n "FabAuthManager configured (expect >= 1): "
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv AIRFLOW__CORE__AUTH_MANAGER | grep -c 'FabAuthManager'

# NEGATIVE, and only meaningful because the line above was not zero: the dev-only auth manager
# writes its plaintext password file into AIRFLOW_HOME on first init.
echo -n "SimpleAuthManager plaintext password file (expect 0): "
sudo docker exec "$C" sh -c 'ls /opt/airflow/simple_auth_manager_passwords.json.generated 2>/dev/null | wc -l'

# POSITIVE: the metadata connection points at the private managed database VM, with the psycopg
# dialect, and not at a container on this host.
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv AIRFLOW__DATABASE__SQL_ALCHEMY_CONN | sed 's#//[^@]*@#//<redacted>@#'

# POSITIVE: no bundled postgres and no redis snuck in from the upstream compose.
sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'

# POSITIVE: the example DAGs are off, so the DAG list is the user's own.
echo -n "load_examples (expect False): "
sudo docker exec "$C" printenv AIRFLOW__CORE__LOAD_EXAMPLES
```
